problems.title: The Trust Crisis of the AI Era
problems.subtitle: Creation has grown exponentially; the ability to prove authorship has stood still.

cards.title: Creations are copied, provenance is unprovable
cards.painPoint: AI images, video and text are created, shared and commercialized at scale, yet it is hard to prove who made them, with which model, under what parameters, when, and without plagiarizing training data.
cards.solution: It freezes the entire creative process into a cryptographically verifiable evidence chain that any party can verify independently, outside the original environment.

cards.title: Attestation tools don't know AI; AI tools don't attest
cards.painPoint: Blockchain notarization stores hashes without understanding semantics; AI tools produce content without keeping process records. The two communities talk past each other, with no translation layer between them.
cards.solution: AEP is that translation layer between cryptographic attestation and AI creation, providing a complete, unified evidence system for the creative process.

cards.title: Compliance and courts are waiting for a technical answer
cards.painPoint: AI content labeling is now a mandatory national standard; courts face three hurdles in AI cases—fact-finding, legal application, and liability attribution—while existing evidence only proves "a file existed at some time."
cards.solution: It turns the creative process into structured evidence admissible to courts and regulators, underpinning compliance obligations and legal proof.

aigc.title: Who owns the copyright to AI-generated content?
aigc.subtitle: Purely AI-generated work with no human involvement is not protected by copyright; AEP turns "human intellectual contribution" into verifiable process evidence.
aigc.lead: Copyright law and judicial practice establish that a work must reflect a natural person's original intellectual input. Issuing a single command to an AI is merely advisory assistance, not authorship.
aigc.negativeRule: Content generated solely from simple, generic instructions, without any personalized intervention or selection and wholly produced by AI at random, lacks originality, does not constitute a work, and is not protected by copyright law.
aigc.factorsTitle: The four yardsticks courts use to assess originality

factors.name: Prompt design
factors.desc: Personalized, specific choices about theme, style, composition, wording, and scene detail, rather than a simple generic instruction.

factors.name: Parameter & model control
factors.desc: Tuning core parameters such as composition ratio, clarity, style weight, iteration steps, and random seed, showing control over the result.

factors.name: Multi-round curation
factors.desc: Comparing, rejecting, and retaining multiple candidate outputs based on creative intent and personal aesthetic judgment.

factors.name: Post-generation human editing
factors.desc: Materially modifying, editing, polishing, or restructuring the AI output into the final expression.

aigc.signalTitle: An independently verifiable originality / copyright signal
aigc.signalDesc: The four-factor process evidence is digitally signed, timestamped, and on-chain anchored, then sealed into a standard .aep package exportable to courts, notaries, or copyright registries.
citations: U.S. Copyright Office AI Registration Guidance (2023)
aigc.disclaimer: AEP provides objective, neutral cryptographic process evidence and does not substitute for a court's final determination of originality in any given case.

protocol.title: Attestation & Evidence Exchange Protocol Specification
protocol.subtitle: Attestation & Evidence Exchange Protocol (AEP) · AI-Native Evidence Infrastructure Standard
overview: The Attestation & Evidence Exchange Protocol (AEP) is an open evidence infrastructure protocol for autonomous AI agents and automated content generation.

Through machine-identity binding, causal time proofs, and cryptographically verifiable evidence chains, AEP freezes the AI creation and execution process into complete evidence that any party can verify independently — bridging the gap between generic notarization and AI creation.
The protocol runs on four cooperating infrastructure services — AEP-PKI, AEP-TSA, AEP-Chain, and Developer IAM — and supports neutral offline verification across the entire lifecycle.

principles.title: Openness
principles.desc: An open protocol and specification; any party can freely build standards-compliant implementations

principles.title: Cryptographically Verifiable
principles.desc: Built on proven cryptography; all claims are independently verifiable without relying on trusted intermediaries

principles.title: Extensibility
principles.desc: Modular layered design supporting custom signature schemes and verifiable data structures

principles.title: Interoperability
principles.desc: Natively compatible with MCP, C2PA, and W3C PROV to seamlessly integrate into agent frameworks

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.desc: A set of cryptographically verifiable claims, the atomic unit of the protocol

concepts.title: Artifact
concepts.desc: Code, files, execution decisions, and data generated by AI agents

concepts.title: Event
concepts.desc: Granular execution records, tool invocations, and environment context

concepts.title: Identity
concepts.desc: Agent machine identity credential powered by AEP PKI

concepts.title: Evidence Graph
concepts.desc: A causal graph of events and artifacts, fully capturing the agent's action chain

concepts.title: Blockchain Anchor
concepts.desc: Evidence fingerprints anchored to global distributed ledgers, providing public existence and immutable finality

protocol.levelsSubtitle: From L0 to L7, evidence strength increases progressively (cumulative)

levels.desc: PlainHash: any valid package payload with cryptographic hash for single-point integrity
Signed: at least one valid asymmetric signature providing tamper-proofing and signer attribution
IdentityBound: identity verified via AEP-PKI certificate chain or IdP binding to establish machine principal
Timestamped: high-precision AEP-TSA trusted timestamp proof (RFC 3161) locking causal sequencing
Anchored: AEP-Chain distributed global ledger existence anchoring for immutable finality
Notarized: endorsement by a neutral audit or notary authority
Continuously-witnessed: continuous full-lifecycle execution logs with multi-party consensus witnessing
Hardware-rooted: TEE secure enclave and hardware root of trust binding

protocol.levelsStatus: Current reference implementation (aep-refimpl) has production-grade L0–L2; L3 trusted timestamping and L4 blockchain anchoring are verified end-to-end; L5–L7 remain reserved protocol tiers.

standards.title: Evidence MCP
standards.desc: MCP is the de facto standard for agent-tool interaction; AEP treats Evidence MCP as a native core integration gateway to empower agents with native evidence capabilities.

standards.title: C2PA
standards.desc: C2PA focuses on media content provenance (Content Credentials), while AEP concentrates on verifiable evidence chains across the full lifecycle of AI agent executions. The two are complementary.

standards.title: W3C PROV
standards.desc: PROV provides a general provenance ontology specification. AEP's evidence graph closely aligns with its data model while being cryptographically optimized for AI behaviors.

architecture.title: System Architecture
architecture.subtitle: Attestation & Evidence Exchange Protocol (AEP) · Five-Layer Technical Stack and Infrastructure Matrix
overview: The Attestation & Evidence Exchange Protocol (AEP) is engineered on a decoupled, layered design to provide standardized and cryptographically verifiable evidence chains for AI Agent executions and automated assets.

Addressing core pain points such as tamper-prone text logs and post-hoc snapshots that lose causal context, AEP defines a five-layer stack: Evidence MCP captures behaviors and events, which are then combined with Merkle proofs, asymmetric signatures, and timestamps, and packaged into standard .aep evidence packages.

At the infrastructure tier, AEP integrates AEP-PKI, AEP-TSA, AEP-Chain, and Developer IAM as four complementary infrastructure services, covering machine identity issuance, causal ordering, and immutable state anchoring.

layers.name: AI Application Layer
layers.desc: Application layer: autonomous agents, multi-agent workflows, and tool platforms

layers.name: Evidence Capture Layer
layers.desc: Capture layer: Evidence MCP, SDK interceptors, and runtime environment probes

layers.name: Evidence Model Layer
layers.desc: Model layer: structured evidence, causal events, and machine identity models

layers.name: Cryptographic Layer
layers.desc: Cryptographic layer: asymmetric signatures, hash digests, Merkle trees, RFC 3161 timestamps

layers.name: Verification Layer
layers.desc: Verification layer: neutral verifiers, offline verification tools, and objective audit reports

architecture.graphDesc: The evidence graph uses a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to accurately capture the agent execution trail: Events link Artifacts and Identities via generatedBy/used semantics, while precededBy locks causal sequencing.
architecture.dataflowSubtitle: Complete closed loop from action capture to independent verification
dataflowSteps: AI Agent executes mission-critical tasks and triggers action capture
Evidence MCP captures and standardizes Artifacts and Events
Compute cryptographic hash digests of artifacts and events
Generate asymmetric digital signatures using agent private key
Build causal graphs and construct Merkle integrity proofs
Seal and package into standardized .aep evidence container
Any third party verifies independently offline or online
architecture.packageDesc: The .aep evidence package is a standardized, out-of-the-box container that bundles manifest specifications, identity metadata, artifact digests, causal event chains, Merkle proofs, and digital signatures.

security.title: Security Model
security.subtitle: Zero-trust security based on cryptographic verifiability
modelText: AEP's security design centers on one core philosophy: providing an objective, verifiable evidence infrastructure rather than subjectively endorsing the veracity of content conclusions. The protocol assumes no centralized trust, but enables any entity to objectively audit and trace an Agent's identity, timestamp window, and data integrity independently of the execution environment.

All security properties are grounded in rigorous asymmetric cryptography, collision-resistant hashing, Merkle tree proofs, and RFC 3161 timestamping mechanisms, making unauthorized alterations or forgeries cryptographically undeniable.

crypto.title: SM2 / Asymmetric Digital Signatures
crypto.desc: Discrete logarithm and elliptic curve cryptography for execution identity authenticity and non-repudiation

crypto.title: SM3 / Cryptographic Hash Algorithm
crypto.desc: 256-bit secure hash digest guaranteeing avalanche-effect integrity verification across all inputs

crypto.title: Merkle Tree Existence Proofs
crypto.desc: Efficient proof of membership supporting high-throughput independent verification of large-scale action records

crypto.title: AEP TSA Trusted Timestamp
crypto.desc: High-precision causal time sequencing (RFC 3161) providing time proofs for ordering validation and replay detection

threats.desc: Before data is hashed and signed, an attacker injects into memory or uses a debugger/Rootkit to alter prompts, parameters, or outputs, producing formally valid but false evidence.
threats.mitigation: Millisecond incremental signing + Merkle-chain avalanche checks + periodic environment-hash refresh, shrinking the tampering window and exposing any change instantly.

threats.desc: After stealing a signing key, an attacker forges evidence, replays old signatures, or repudiates existing ones.
threats.mitigation: Keys are encrypted at rest with HSM/TEE hardware protection; trusted timestamps bound the leak time, verified against certificate revocation (CRL/OCSP).

threats.desc: Crafted .aep containers (zip bombs, path traversal, deep nesting) attack the verifier to trigger crashes or code execution.
threats.mitigation: Memory-safe implementation, fuzzing, decompression-ratio and path-traversal checks, and sandboxed parsing.

threats.desc: Constructing hash collisions to bypass integrity checks, or coercing weak algorithms during negotiation to lower evidence strength.
threats.mitigation: Collision-resistant hashes and a minimum 128-bit security policy; negotiation takes the strongest common set and alerts on downgrades.

flowSteps.desc: Deconstruct .aep container hierarchy, validate directory specs, and enforce path-traversal protection
Extract object topology, construct causal graphs, and enforce directed acyclic properties
Strictly validate schema compliance and field correctness of events, artifacts, and metadata
Independently recompute Merkle root hashes to verify dataset integrity and consistency
Validate asymmetric signatures and validity against public keys and AEP PKI certificate chains
Evaluate cryptographic assurance and external anchoring state to determine evidence level (cumulative L0–L7; reference implementation currently covers L0–L4, with L5–L7 reserved)
Generate machine-readable structured audit reports (supporting JSON / SARIF / HTML)

statements: AEP provides neutral, cryptographic evidence infrastructure: evidence is independently verifiable, transparently traceable, and fully auditable across its lifecycle.
Security relies on modern public-key cryptography and hash collision resistance; signature forgery and hash inversion are computationally infeasible.
Agent private key and certificate lifecycle management are foundational; securing private keys is essential for non-repudiation.
AEP focuses on the chain of evidence (Proof of AI Action), making all unauthorized modifications and impersonations mathematically detectable.
